notes.meaning: David had just walked past the summit of the Mount of Olives when Ziba, the servant managing Mephibosheth's estate, came out to meet him. Ziba brought two donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of flat bread, dried fruit, raisins, and a large goatskin filled with wine. Though the food was very welcome to the fleeing king, Ziba used this generous gift to win David's favor for selfish gain.

David asked Ziba what all the supplies were for. Ziba answered with great politeness that the donkeys were for the royal family to ride, the food was for the servants, and the wine was to revive anyone who grew faint in the wilderness. Ziba made himself seem like a thoughtful and loyal friend when David was at his lowest point.

When David asked why Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was not with him, Ziba told a bold lie. He claimed Mephibosheth stayed behind in Jerusalem, expecting Israel to hand Saul's old kingdom back to him during the chaos. It was an absurd story, but David was in deep grief and believed it.

Without checking the facts or hearing Mephibosheth's side, David made a hasty and unfair ruling by handing all of Mephibosheth's land over to Ziba. Ziba bowed low and pretended to care only about having the king's favor. David let his troubled emotions lead him into cheating a loyal, innocent friend to reward a schemer.

As David neared the village of Bahurim, a relative of King Saul named Shimei came out against him. Shimei harbored long-standing hatred against David for replacing Saul's royal family on the throne. Now that David was running for his life, Shimei felt safe to shout vile curses at him openly.

Shimei threw rocks at David and his officials along the road. Even though David's experienced soldiers and bodyguards marched all around him, Shimei dared to pelt them from a distance. He showed utter contempt for the king when David was at his weakest.

Shimei screamed that David was a worthless man of bloodshed who was finally getting what he deserved. He claimed the Lord was punishing David for the deaths in Saul's family and giving the kingdom to Absalom. In truth, David was innocent of murdering Saul's relatives, but Shimei used the family tragedy to fuel his own bitter revenge.

David's fierce nephew Abishai was furious that such a low, worthless man would insult the king. He called Shimei a dead dog, a term used for the most contemptible creature, and asked permission to march across and chop off his head. Abishai wanted to defend the king's honor immediately with the sword.

David told Abishai and his brother Joab to stand down and not interfere. Even though Shimei's specific accusations were false, David knew his conscience was guilty of other sins, and he saw God's chastening hand in this humiliation. God did not put sin in Shimei's heart, but by His providence He allowed Shimei to vent his malice to humble the king.

David explained his patience by reminding his men that his own flesh and blood, Absalom, was trying to murder him. If his own son wanted his life, it was no surprise that a relative of Saul would shout insults. David told them to leave Shimei alone because God had permitted this painful trial.

David trusted that the Lord would notice his misery and David's humble acceptance of this rebuke. He held on to the hope that God would eventually turn this unfair cursing into a blessing. Bearing abuse patiently before God is often the very path that leads to His mercy.

David and his men continued marching down the road while Shimei kept pace on the ridge of the opposite hill. The entire way, Shimei never stopped yelling curses, hurling stones, and tossing clouds of dirt into the air. David bore this public abuse in silence without fighting back.

David and his exhausted followers finally arrived at a resting place beyond the hills, away from Shimei's shouting. There they were able to stop, rest, and recover their strength. Even in the middle of deep sorrow, God provided a quiet shelter where the king could be refreshed.

While David fled, Absalom and his rebel followers entered Jerusalem unopposed. Ahithophel, the renowned and wise advisor who had betrayed David, was right by Absalom's side. Absalom felt triumphant, believing that taking the capital meant the kingdom was already his.

David's loyal friend Hushai arrived in Jerusalem to carry out David's secret plan. He approached Absalom and cheered loudly, calling out long life to the king. Absalom was led to believe that another of David's closest advisors had decided to switch sides.

Absalom was suspicious and asked Hushai why he had abandoned David. He questioned whether this was how a true friend showed loyalty. Absalom called David Hushai's friend rather than his own father, showing how cold his own heart was toward David.

Hushai gave a clever, double-edged reply to win Absalom's trust. He claimed he would serve whomever the Lord and the people had chosen to rule. Hushai spoke words that made Absalom think he meant him, while in his heart Hushai still considered David God's true anointed king.

Hushai added that it was completely natural for him to serve the son just as he had faithfully served the father. This flattering reasoning completely satisfied Absalom's pride. Absalom was entirely fooled and welcomed David's secret friend into his inner circle of advisors.

Absalom gathered his leaders and called on Ahithophel to give counsel on their next step. Having seized the palace, Absalom wanted a solid plan to secure the throne and rally the nation behind him. He relied on human cleverness instead of seeking guidance from God.

Ahithophel advised Absalom to publicly sleep with the concubines David had left behind to manage the palace. Taking over a king's harem was an ancient way of claiming his royal power, and it would show that father and son could never be reconciled. Ahithophel knew this scandalous act would force Absalom's followers to fight to the death because there was no turning back.

A tent was pitched for Absalom on the palace flat roof, where he went in to his father's concubines in front of all Israel. This terrible sin took place on the exact roof where David had first looked with lust upon Bathsheba. In this dark moment, God's warning through the prophet Nathan came true, showing that God's word never fails.

In those times, Ahithophel's advice was treated with the same awe and respect as if someone had asked an oracle from God. Both David and Absalom trusted his political genius completely. Yet worldly wisdom without the fear of God can quickly lead leaders into ruinous and wicked counsel.
